chapter_title: Certification Prep: Lighting, Environment & Optimization Review
chapter_summary:
The `Lighting & Cameras`, `Environment Art`, and `Optimization` domains are where your artistic vision truly comes to life and is then made performant. These sections of the Unity Certified 3D Artist exam test your ability to create visually stunning scenes that also run efficiently across target platforms. Understanding the interplay between lighting, environment design, and performance is critical, as a beautiful but unoptimized scene is often unusable in a real game.

For `Lighting & Cameras`, a deep understanding of Unity's lighting pipeline is essential. You need to differentiate between **real-time lighting** (dynamic, flexible, but performance-intensive) and **baked lighting** (static, performant, but inflexible at runtime). **Mixed lighting** offers a balance, allowing some lights to be baked and others real-time. The exam will likely test your knowledge of how to set up `Lightmap Static` objects for baking, configure `Lightmap Parameters`, and use `Light Probes` to provide baked lighting information to dynamic objects. Each light type—`Directional Light` (simulates distant sun), `Point Light` (omnidirectional, like a bulb), `Spot Light` (cone-shaped, like a flashlight), and `Area Light` (rectangular, for soft, diffuse light)—has specific artistic uses and performance characteristics. `Reflection Probes` are also crucial for capturing and applying reflections to PBR materials, making surfaces look more integrated with their environment. Common mistakes include relying too heavily on real-time lights for static scenes (leading to poor performance) or neglecting to set up `Light Probes` for dynamic objects, resulting in them looking unlit or out of place.

`Environment Art` focuses on how you construct compelling 3D worlds. This includes principles of `Scene Composition` (e.g., rule of thirds, leading lines, visual hierarchy) to guide the player's eye and create atmosphere. You should be familiar with Unity's `Terrain` system for creating landscapes, including sculpting tools, painting textures, and adding trees and details. The concept of `Modular Assets` is vital: creating reusable pieces (e.g., wall sections, pillars, rocks) that can be combined and reconfigured to build larger, varied environments efficiently. This not only saves time but also improves performance by allowing for better batching. Questions might involve identifying best practices for creating seamless modular assets or optimizing terrain details.

Finally, `Optimization` is a cross-cutting concern. As a 3D artist, you are directly responsible for creating assets and scenes that perform well. Key techniques include:
*   **Level of Detail (LOD) Groups:** Creating multiple versions of a mesh with decreasing polygon counts, which Unity swaps out based on distance from the camera. This significantly reduces rendering overhead for distant objects.
*   **Occlusion Culling:** A system that prevents Unity from rendering objects that are completely hidden behind other objects from the camera's perspective. It requires baking `Occlusion Culling` data into your scene.
*   **Draw Call Reduction:** Minimizing the number of times the CPU tells the GPU to draw something. This is achieved through techniques like `Static Batching` (combining static meshes that share materials), `Dynamic Batching` (combining small dynamic meshes), and `Texture Atlasing` (packing multiple textures into one to reduce material count).
*   **Mesh Optimization:** Reducing polygon count where possible, using efficient UV layouts, and avoiding unnecessary sub-meshes.
*   **Texture Optimization:** Using appropriate compression, resolutions, and `Mip Maps`.

A common mistake is to ignore optimization until the very end of a project, leading to difficult and time-consuming fixes. Artists should consider performance from the outset, making informed decisions about asset complexity and scene setup. Safety notes include understanding that aggressive optimization can sometimes lead to visual degradation; always test changes thoroughly to ensure a balance between performance and visual quality.

screens.title: Lighting, Environment & Optimization Review
screens.subtitle: Prepare visuals that look great and run well — lighting, terrain, modular assets, and performance techniques.

narration.text: In this lesson you will connect artistic decisions to technical constraints. We'll review how real-time, baked, and mixed lighting affect both look and performance, and how light probes and reflection probes help dynamic objects fit into a baked world. You will also revisit environment craft: composing scenes, sculpting terrain, and building modular assets that scale. Finally, we'll cover optimization techniques you must apply as an artist — level of detail groups, occlusion culling, draw call reduction, and texture and mesh optimization. Each section includes a concrete workflow or hands-on step you can practice in Unity: marking geometry as Lightmap Static and baking, creating LOD levels and testing transitions, and baking occlusion to prevent rendering hidden objects. This review is practical: it ties visual goals to measurable performance outcomes so you can make balanced trade-offs. By the end you'll be able to choose the right lighting strategy for static and dynamic scenes, design modular assets that batch efficiently, and use LOD and occlusion to keep frame rates healthy without sacrificing the visual story. Think about a static interior you want to polish — what would you bake first, and which objects need probes or LODs?

keyIdea.title: Balance look and performance
keyIdea.text: Good art starts with intent: choose baked lighting for static detail, use probes for dynamic objects, and plan LODs and batching early to preserve both fidelity and frame rate.

screens.title: Real-time vs Baked vs Mixed Lighting
screens.subtitle: Understand the trade-offs between flexibility and performance.

narration.text: First, define the three lighting approaches so you can select the right one. Real-time lighting is calculated each frame and therefore supports dynamic objects and moving lights. Use it when lights or shadows must change during gameplay. A concrete example is a flashlight carried by the player; the cone and shadows must update immediately. Baked lighting is precomputed and stored in lightmaps for static geometry. It produces high-quality global illumination and soft shadows with minimal runtime cost. For example, a static interior with complex indirect light should use baked lightmaps to get realistic lighting without expensive per-frame calculations. Mixed lighting blends the two: some light information is baked while direct or shadow information remains dynamic, giving a balance between cost and flexibility. A common misconception is to default to real-time for visual fidelity; this can drastically increase performance cost when the scene is mostly static. Another pitfall is baking dynamic objects as static by mistake, which makes them look incorrectly lit at runtime. The takeaway is a decision heuristic: bake where geometry and lighting are static, use probes for dynamic objects, and reserve real-time lights for motion and interactivity. Which parts of your scene truly need motion-driven lighting?

keyIdea.title: Choose by motion
keyIdea.text: If lights or objects move, favor real-time or mixed. If everything is static, bake to save runtime cost.

content.html:
Core Concept Real-time vs Baked vs Mixed
Lighting pipeline comparison
Define each approach, example use, and common misconception.
Definitions & Examples
  • Real-time: Dynamic per-frame lighting. Example: player flashlight that must update shadows as you move.
  • Baked: Precomputed lightmaps for static geometry. Example: a static interior with complex indirect light.
  • Mixed: Bake indirect lighting while keeping direct shadows or key lights dynamic for interaction.
Common mistake
Relying on real-time lights for mostly static scenes increases runtime cost unnecessarily.
Editor checklist (practice steps)
// Editor steps - not API calls, just workflow
1. Identify static geometry (walls, floors, large props).
2. Mark those objects as Lightmap Static in the Inspector.
3. Place Light Probes for moving actors near their paths.
4. Configure Lightmap Parameters and run a bake.
5. Play and verify dynamic objects sample probes and look coherent.
Key Takeaway

Bake static light, probe dynamic objects, and reserve real-time for motion to balance fidelity and performance.

screens.title: Light Types and Their Uses
screens.subtitle: Directional, Point, Spot, and Area lights — artistic intent and performance notes.

narration.text: Understanding light types helps you place lights that support mood without surprising performance costs. Directional light simulates distant sources like the sun; it affects all geometry uniformly and is commonly used for outdoor scenes and overall scene illumination. A practical example is using a directional light for midday sun with a hard shadow to communicate time of day. Point lights are omnidirectional and behave like bulbs; they are useful for interior lamps but can be expensive if many are active in real-time. A common mistake is placing many overlapping point lights without baking or culling, which increases per-frame cost. Spot lights create a cone of light and are ideal for flashlights, stage lights, or focused accents — they often need to cast precise shadows when used dynamically. Area lights produce soft diffuse illumination across a rectangular surface and are great for photographic softbox effects, but in many pipelines area lights are baked or approximated because real-time rectangular area lights are heavy. Reflection probes capture surroundings for PBR reflections and are critical for materials to look integrated; neglecting probes leaves shiny materials looking flat. When you design lighting, ask: which lights must move, and which can be baked? That answer should guide whether you choose directional, point, spot, or area lights in each case.

keyIdea.title: Match light to intent
keyIdea.text: Pick the light type that achieves the visual goal with the least runtime cost: directional for sun, point for bulbs, spot for cones, area for soft fills (usually baked).

content.html:
Definition Light Types
Directional, Point, Spot, Area & Probes
Directional Light
Simulates distant sun; good for global illumination and outdoor scenes.
Point Light
Omnidirectional bulb; ideal for lamps and local illumination.
Spot Light
Cone-shaped light for flashlights and stage effects; good for focused highlights.
Area Light
Rectangular soft fill used for photographic softboxes; often baked or approximated due to cost.
Reflection & Light Probes
Probes sample baked lighting and environment reflections so dynamic objects and PBR materials match the scene.
Mistake to avoid: forgetting probes for moving characters, which makes them look unlit in a baked scene.
Key Takeaway

Match light type to the artistic need: directional for sun, point for bulbs, spot for cones, area for soft fills; add probes to integrate dynamic objects.

screens.title: Baking Lighting: Editor Workflow
screens.subtitle: Mark static geometry, place probes, configure parameters, and run a bake.

narration.text: Let's walk through a practical bake workflow you can replicate in a small scene. Start by identifying static geometry: walls, floors, stairs, and large props that will not move. Mark those objects as Lightmap Static in the Inspector so the baking system includes them. Next, configure Lightmap Parameters: choose a resolution and indirect sample quality appropriate to your target platform, keeping in mind that higher settings increase bake time. Place a Light Probe Group along player paths and near dynamic props so moving objects sample baked indirect light. Add Reflection Probes in areas with shiny materials—inside rooms or near polished surfaces—to capture local reflections. Now run the bake. Observe the generated lightmaps and compare the cost: lower the resolution if you need faster build times. A common misconception is to expect a single perfect bake; in practice you iterate: adjust probe density, tweak lightmap parameters, and rebake until dynamic objects visually match static lighting. Finally, test the scene in Play mode and watch dynamic objects. If they appear disconnected from the environment, add more probes or adjust probe placement. The closing question: after your first bake, what visual mismatch would indicate you need additional probes or a different parameter set?

keyIdea.title: Iterate bakes
keyIdea.text: Baking is an iterative process: mark static objects, place probes, run a bake, and adjust parameters until dynamic objects integrate convincingly.

content.html:
Process Flow Lighting Bake Workflow
Step-by-step bake checklist
A repeatable sequence for consistent bakes.
Editor Checklist (practice in a simple scene)
// Bake workflow - conceptual steps
1. Identify and mark static geometry: Inspector -> Lightmap Static
2. Place Light Probe Group near dynamic paths and actors
3. Add Reflection Probes in rooms and polished areas
4. Configure Lightmap Parameters: texels per unit, sample counts
5. Run Bake and inspect lightmaps and probe influence
6. Iterate: increase probes or lower resolution based on visual and memory cost
  • Concrete example: mark an interior's walls and furniture as static and place probes at chest height along navigation routes.
  • Misconception: a single probe grid always suffices — probe density matters near high-contrast lighting changes.
  • Takeaway: test in Play mode to verify dynamic objects sample probes correctly.
Example: Interior bake
Mark floor, walls, large props as Lightmap Static. Place probes along corridors. Add one reflection probe per room. Run a low-resolution test bake, adjust, then use final settings for release.
Key Takeaway

Plan static geometry and probes before baking; iterate with quick bakes to converge on quality and performance.

screens.title: Setting Up LOD Groups
screens.subtitle: Create multiple mesh levels and tune transition percentages to reduce rendering cost at distance.

narration.text: Level of Detail groups let Unity swap simpler meshes for complex ones as distance increases, directly reducing vertex and fragment cost. A clear workflow helps: create three versions of your model — full-detail LOD0, mid-detail LOD1, and low-detail LOD2 — ensuring each version preserves the silhouette where it matters. Add an LOD Group component to the root object and drag each renderer into the correct LOD slot. Configure transition percentages so LOD0 remains visible when the object is close, LOD1 appears at mid-range, and LOD2 at far distances. A practical example is a rock asset: up close you want full geometry, but dozens of distant rocks can use LOD2 without visual loss. Common mistakes include very abrupt transitions that cause popping, or using identical meshes that provide no benefit. To avoid popping, stagger transition thresholds and test using the Scene view's LOD Debug to watch swaps in action. Also ensure each LOD's renderer is correctly assigned and that materials are shared where possible to enable batching. The final check is performance: verify draw calls and frame time before and after adding LODs. How would you choose thresholds if a player can approach objects quickly versus in a slow exploration game?

keyIdea.title: Swap complexity by distance
keyIdea.text: Design LODs to preserve silhouette and material sharing; test transitions to avoid popping and to maximize performance benefit.

content.html:
Process Flow LOD Groups
Create and tune LODs for cost savings
Step-by-step
  1. Create LOD0, LOD1, LOD2 meshes preserving silhouette.
  2. Add LOD Group component to the parent object.
  3. Drag each mesh's Renderer into the corresponding LOD slot.
  4. Set transition percentages (e.g., 70%, 30%, 10%) and test in Scene view with LOD Debug.
  5. Share materials across LODs to enable batching where possible.
Key Takeaway

Design LODs to reduce polygon cost while preserving perceived shape; test thresholds in the Scene view debugger.

Concrete example: Rock cluster
LOD0: full sculpt. LOD1: simplified topology with preserved silhouette. LOD2: billboard or very low-poly mesh for extreme distances. Use LOD Debug to watch transitions and avoid abrupt popping by smoothing thresholds.
Common mistake
Assigning incorrect renderers or failing to share materials — this prevents batching and reduces the performance benefit of LODs.

screens.title: Occlusion Culling: Bake and Visualize
screens.subtitle: Prevent drawing objects hidden behind geometry to cut GPU work.

narration.text: Occlusion culling stops the renderer from drawing objects the camera cannot see because they are hidden behind other geometry. The practical workflow is straightforward: mark static geometry as Static, open the Occlusion Culling window, choose a voxel size that balances bake time and culling precision, and click Bake. Smaller voxels increase accuracy but take longer to compute. After baking, use the Visualization tab while moving the Scene view camera to see which objects are culled in real time. An example: in a building with many rooms and corridors, properly baked occlusion prevents the engine from rendering entire rooms that are off-camera. A common misconception is that occlusion culling will hide everything behind the nearest wall regardless of camera movement, but occlusion relies on baked data and camera position; dynamic objects or incorrectly marked static objects may not be culled. Also, marking highly detailed small props as static can increase bake complexity; focus on large occluders like walls, floors, and big props. The final check is to play the scene and confirm reduced draw calls when moving around occluding geometry. Which large scene elements act as natural occluders in your levels?

keyIdea.title: Use occlusion wisely
keyIdea.text: Bake occlusion against large static geometry to stop rendering hidden objects; verify with visualization and balance voxel size for accuracy and build time.

content.html:
Process Flow Occlusion Culling
Bake occlusion and validate with visualization
Bake steps
  1. Mark large, static geometry as Static so occlusion data includes it.
  2. Open Window → Rendering → Occlusion Culling and switch to the Bake tab.
  3. Set Voxel Size and Backface Tolerance and click Bake.
  4. Use the Visualization tab in Scene view to confirm which objects are culled as you move the camera.
Example
In a multi-room interior, bake occlusion so rooms not visible to the camera aren't rendered, reducing draw and fragment cost.
Visualization tips
Move the Scene view camera and watch the culling overlay: culled objects are not drawn. If dynamic actors are culled incorrectly, ensure they are not marked static or adjust bake settings.
Key Takeaway

Bake occlusion against large static occluders and verify results with the visualization tools to ensure correct culling and improved performance.

screens.title: Draw Call Reduction Techniques
screens.subtitle: Static batching, dynamic batching, and texture atlasing compared.

narration.text: Draw calls are a key performance metric: each draw call is a C P U instruction for the G P U to render some geometry. Three artistic techniques reduce draw calls. Static batching combines multiple static meshes that share the same material into larger combined meshes, dramatically lowering draw calls for level geometry. For example, repeated decorative props that don't move benefit from static batching. Dynamic batching groups small dynamic meshes at runtime but works best with simple vertex counts and shared materials; it is limited and not a substitute for static batching. Texture atlasing packs many small textures into a single larger texture so multiple objects can share one material, enabling batching and fewer draw calls. A common mistake is increasing atlas size without considering memory or mip maps; atlasing reduces draw calls but can increase memory if not handled carefully. Another pitfall is creating atlases that prevent reuse of textures across different material variants. The practical workflow: group what can be static and share materials, create atlases for repeated small assets, and measure draw calls before and after changes. The guiding question: are your draw call savings worth the texture size and memory trade-offs for your target platform?

keyIdea.title: Reduce draw calls strategically
keyIdea.text: Static batching and atlases reduce draw calls for static, repeated assets; dynamic batching helps small moving objects but has limitations.

content.html:
Comparison Draw Call Techniques
Static Batching · Dynamic Batching · Texture Atlasing
Static Batching
Combines static meshes that share materials to reduce draw calls. Best for static level pieces like walls, floors, and repeated props.
Mistake: marking everything static prevents dynamic movement and can increase memory usage.
Dynamic Batching
Groups small dynamic meshes at runtime. Useful for many small moving objects but limited by vertex counts and not a silver bullet.
Tip: keep vertex counts low and share simple materials.
Texture Atlasing
Pack many small textures into one to reduce unique materials and enable batching. Carefully choose atlas sizes and mip map settings for target platforms.
Common pitfall: atlases that are too large for mobile memory budgets.
Quick Checklist
Share materials, atlas repeated small textures, mark truly static geometry for static batching, and measure draw calls in the profiler to confirm gains.

screens.title: Mesh and Texture Optimization
screens.subtitle: Reduce polygon count, optimize UVs, and choose compression and mip maps wisely.

narration.text: Mesh and texture optimization are artist responsibilities that directly affect rendering and memory. Mesh optimization means reducing polygon counts where detail isn’t needed, creating efficient UV layouts, and avoiding unnecessary sub-meshes that create extra materials and draw calls. For example, a background prop can often use far fewer vertices than a hero object while preserving perceived shape. Texture optimization involves choosing appropriate resolutions, applying compression formats suited to the platform, and enabling mip maps so distant textures sample cheaper smaller levels. A common error is leaving very high-resolution textures for tiny objects visible only at a distance — this wastes memory without visual benefit. Another pitfall is poor UV packing that wastes texel density; allocate higher density to hero assets and lower density to background props. Always test visual quality after compression and on target hardware to check for banding or artifacting. The key trade-off is visual fidelity versus memory and bandwidth: reduce what the player cannot discern and preserve detail where it matters most. Ask yourself: which assets are in the player's focus and deserve higher texel density? Mesh and Texture Optimization means lower polygon counts and texture resolutions for distant or peripheral assets; keep detail where the player focuses to save memory and rendering cost.. In practical terms, reduce polygon count, optimize uvs, and choose compression and mip maps wisely.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Optimize for perception
keyIdea.text: Lower polygon counts and texture resolutions for distant or peripheral assets; keep detail where the player focuses to save memory and rendering cost.

content.html:
Core Concept Mesh & Texture Optimization
Efficient geometry and texture use
Mesh Optimization
  • Reduce polys where silhouette is preserved.
  • Use LODs for distant objects.
  • Avoid unnecessary sub-meshes that create separate materials.
Example: background furniture can be much simpler than nearby interactive props.
Texture Optimization
  • Pick resolution by perceived size in game and target platform memory.
  • Use compression formats suitable to platform and enable mip maps.
  • Pack textures into atlases when it reduces material count without harming quality.
Mistake: high-res textures on tiny objects waste bandwidth and memory.
Key Takeaway

Optimize where players look: reduce asset complexity outside focus and test changes on target hardware to validate quality and savings.

screens.title: Scene Composition & Modular Assets
screens.subtitle: Use composition rules and modular building blocks to guide the player's eye and support performance.

narration.text: Scene composition is the arrangement of visual elements to create hierarchy, guide attention, and support gameplay. Basic principles like the rule of thirds, leading lines, and focal contrast help you direct the player's eye. For environment art, combine composition with modular assets: build reusable sections like wall segments, doorways, and props that fit together seamlessly. Modular design saves time and promotes batching because identical parts can share materials. A concrete scenario: use modular wall sections and varied props to create many unique rooms while only authoring a small library of parts. Terrain tools are part of environment art too: sculpt large landforms with Unity's Terrain system, paint blended textures, and add trees and details sparingly where they matter for composition and performance. Common mistakes include over-detailing modular pieces so they lose benefits of batching, or placing too many unique materials which fragments draw calls. The production insight is to design modular pieces with consistent UV scale and material usage so you can tile them, atlas their textures, and let the renderer batch where possible. How could you limit unique material instances while keeping enough visual variation?

keyIdea.title: Design for reuse
keyIdea.text: Compose scenes with modular parts and composition rules so art supports both storytelling and efficient rendering.

content.html:
Definition Composition & Modularity
Compose purposeful levels with reusable pieces
Composition Principles
  • Rule of thirds and focal points help prioritize what the player sees first.
  • Leading lines and contrast guide movement and attention.
  • Place visual anchors to support navigation and storytelling.
Modular Asset Workflow
Create reusable pieces with consistent pivot points and UV scale. Combine pieces in different arrangements to build varied spaces without many unique materials.
Tip: design modular pieces for batching by sharing materials and avoiding unique textures per piece.
Key Takeaway

Good composition and modular design let you scale visual fidelity while keeping materials and draw calls manageable.

screens.title: Activity: Implement LODs and Bake Occlusion
screens.subtitle: A guided lab to see performance impact in a simple scene.

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks you through setting up LODs and baking occlusion in a small Unity scene so you feel the performance difference. Start by importing or duplicating a model to create three LOD meshes: full detail, medium, and low detail. Place several instances in the scene at varying distances from the camera. Add an LOD Group to one instance and assign the three renderers, then copy the setup to the others. Adjust transition percentages so LOD swaps occur progressively. Next, mark the large environment meshes as Static and open the Occlusion Culling window. Choose a voxel size that balances bake time and accuracy for your scene and run Bake. Enter Play mode and move the camera to validate both LOD transitions and occlusion behavior. Use the Scene view LOD Debug and the Occlusion visualization to examine what changes. A common trap is forgetting to share materials across LODs — this prevents batching and reduces the expected performance gain. Finally, observe draw calls and frame timings before and after the changes. The closing reflection: which change produced the largest reduction in draw calls in your test scene?

keyIdea.title: Practice and measure
keyIdea.text: Set up LODs, bake occlusion, and measure draw calls — hands-on validation ensures optimizations actually improve performance.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity LOD & Occlusion Lab
Implement LODs and bake occlusion
Activity Steps
1. Import model; duplicate and reduce detail for LOD0, LOD1, LOD2.
2. Add LOD Group, assign renderers, set transitions (e.g., 70/30/10).
3. Place multiple instances at various distances.
4. Mark static geometry, open Occlusion Culling, set voxel size and bake.
5. Use LOD Debug and Occlusion Visualization to confirm behavior.
6. Measure draw calls before and after changes.
Example expectation
You should see fewer draw calls after static batching and atlas use, and far fewer visible objects when occlusion is effective. LODs will reduce vertex load for distant objects.
Check your understanding

If draw calls do not drop, verify material sharing, static flags, and that LOD renderers are correctly assigned.

screens.title: Optimization Trade-offs and Testing
screens.subtitle: Avoid late-stage optimization and validate visual quality on target hardware.

narration.text: Optimization is not a single action but a set of trade-offs. A frequent mistake is deferring optimization to the end of a project, which makes fixes time-consuming and often forces visual compromises. Instead, consider performance from the outset: plan LODs, share materials, and consider atlas strategies as you art assets. When optimizing, always test on target hardware and measure both frame timings and draw calls. For example, aggressive texture compression might reduce memory but introduce banding on mobile GPUs; test those compressed textures on the device rather than only in the editor. Another trade-off is between bake quality and build time: extremely high-resolution lightmaps look great but may be impractical for team iteration; use quick bakes during iteration and reserve final bakes for release. A common misconception is that optimization is only about polygons; texture resolution, mip maps, and material count are equally important. The practical approach is iterative: make a change, measure, and if the visual cost is unacceptable, try an alternative. Always prioritize what the player sees most. Ask yourself after each pass: did this optimization meaningfully lower C P U/G P U work without harming the player-facing quality?

keyIdea.title: Measure, don't guess
keyIdea.text: Plan optimizations early, test on real hardware, iterate, and prefer changes that reduce measurable CPU or GPU work while preserving key visual quality.

content.html:
Common Mistake Optimization Trade-offs
Plan early, measure often
Trade-offs to consider
  • Bake time vs lightmap quality: iterate with low-res bakes during work.
  • Texture size vs memory: compress and test on target devices.
  • LOD complexity vs visual popping: smooth transitions and test movement speeds.
Testing checklist
Measure draw calls and frame time, test on devices, visualize LOD and occlusion, and compare before/after metrics to validate benefits.
Mistake: optimizing without measurement may move cost to a different subsystem instead of reducing it overall.
Key Takeaway

Optimization decisions should be driven by measurement and player perception; perform small iterative changes and validate on target hardware.

First, choose lighting strategy by motion: bake for static scenes, use real-time for moving lights, and mix the two with probes to bridge dynamic objects. Second, design modular assets and consistent materials to support batching and LOD workflows, which reduce draw calls and speed iteration. Third, optimize iteratively and measure on target hardware: implement LODs and occlusion culling, atlas textures where beneficial, and test compression and bake settings so you maintain visual fidelity while achieving performance targets. What to Remember
Key Concepts
Lighting Strategy

Modular Assets
Reusable pieces with shared materials support batching and scale environments efficiently.
Measure & Iterate

Summary

screens.title: Remember These Practical Rules
screens.subtitle: Short reminders you can use when designing and optimizing scenes.

narration.text: Keep these practical rules as quick decision aids. First, if a scene or light is static, prioritize baking to capture high-quality global illumination without per-frame cost. Second, always place Light Probes for dynamic characters so they inherit baked lighting and avoid feeling out of place. Third, reduce draw calls by sharing materials, static batching, and using texture atlases for repeated small assets. Fourth, implement LOD Groups to lower geometry cost at distance and bake occlusion culling against large static occluders to avoid rendering invisible objects. Finally, test every optimization on the target hardware, since compression, mip maps, and texture sizes behave differently across devices. These rules help you make quick, production-safe choices that preserve the player's experience while meeting platform constraints. Which rule will you apply first in your next scene?

What to Remember
Practical Rules
Bake Static Light
Use lightmaps for scenes that don't require moving lights to gain quality and runtime efficiency.
Use Probes
Place Light and Reflection Probes so dynamic objects and PBR materials match the baked environment.
Reduce Draw Calls
Share materials, static batch, and atlas textures for repeated small assets to cut draw calls.
Final prompt
Before your next build, pick one optimization to test and measure on target hardware. Small, measured steps produce the most reliable results.
